title: Ivo and the Icy Secret
markdown:
Winter had quieted Whispering Creek to a frozen ribbon. Ivo the bridge tinkerer hummed as he came, satchel heavy with fragrant wood the villagers of Sunpetal Meadow needed for their festival stage. At the creek his song faded.

A wide sheet of ice, like a frozen window, covered the bridge he had built. The babble was gone.

"Oh, dear." He ran a hand through his hair and prodded the ice with his boot. Hard as stone. He nudged the supports; the ice held. Glow, his marmalade cat, watched from a sunny rock, amber eyes narrowed.

"This is quite a pickle, Glow." The sun was warm on his shoulders. The ice would not take a cart, and he could not swim the wood across. The problem wanted a different kind of thinking.

He sat on the mossy bank. The sun, a golden eye, warmed the air. Tiny droplets appeared on the ice, like tears. A patch near the bank softened, then ran, then found its old voice — a trickle, familiar and small. The sun was kissing the ice awake.

His gaze fell on a puddle among fallen leaves. Wisps rose from it, like tiny feathers, and vanished.

"The water is trying to fly," Ivo whispered. Not into nothing. Into the air, as something you could sometimes see and then not. He thought of his own breath on a chilly morning, a misty cloud that disappeared. He tossed a stone into the puddle and watched ripples. Solid ice. Flowing water. Invisible steam. All water, behaving differently.

He hurried to his workshop, Glow trotting behind. He fetched a large flat metal sheet and a sturdy brazier. Back at the bridge he lit a small gentle fire, set it near the thickest ice, and laid the metal where the sun could strike it as well.

The sheet grew warm and sent that warmth down. The ice beneath began to hiss and sigh. A channel of clear water opened along the deck, freeing the planks. Steam rose from the warm water; when it touched the cooler fabric of Ivo's tunic, it turned into tiny droplets again.

Not magic. Heat. Ice to water. Water to vapor. Vapor, cooled, to water once more.

He waited until the channel was honest, then pushed the cart along the cleared bridge. The wood reached Sunpetal Meadow. The stage would be built.

On the return, Dr. Kellan the botanist came along the path. "Ivo! A successful trip. That ice looked formidable this morning."

Ivo's eyes sparkled. "It's the changes. The ice — solid — melted to water because of the sun and the brazier's heat. Some of the water flew off as steam, a gas, still water, only spread out. When that steam met my cold tunic, it became drops again."

Dr. Kellan stroked his beard. "The three states: solid, liquid, gas. Temperature invites the dance. Melting, evaporation, condensation. It is happening in kettles and clouds and creeks, whether a tinkerer is watching or not."

Glow purred, as if she had supervised the states of matter personally.

Ivo looked at the last rags of ice, shrinking in the afternoon. He did not ask the trees to remember.

"I wonder," he said, "whether tonight's cold will stitch the creek shut again — and whether the same heat, used earlier, would save us the brazier, or whether winter always gets the last word until spring."

Dr. Kellan's mouth twitched. "Come by the classroom. We'll put a kettle on and watch the window mist. Same story. Smaller creek."
